heroData.title: EOR & PEO Services in Cuba
heroData.subtitle: Navigate state-mandated employment through official Cuban agencies
heroData.description: In Cuba, foreign entities cannot hire local personnel directly. Employment must be managed through specialized state-owned entities (Empresas Empleadoras) like ACOREC or Palco. These agencies act as the legal Employer of Record, managing payroll, taxes, and social security compliance under the unique Cuban regulatory framework.
heroData.bestFor: Foreign companies and representative offices in Cuba

sections.title: Employee Onboarding Workflow
sections.subtitle: Navigating the State Employment Agency System
sections.description: Hiring in Cuba involves a tripartite relationship between the foreign company, the Cuban worker, and the state-owned employment agency.

steps.title: Agency Engagement
steps.description: Identify and sign a service agreement with an authorized Cuban employment agency (e.g., ACOREC for foreign branches, Palco for diplomatic/business groups, or Cubanacán for tourism). This agency will legally employ the workers you select.

steps.title: Talent Selection & Approval
steps.description: While the foreign entity can propose candidates, the state agency must approve them. The agency maintains a 'Cantera' (talent pool) from which workers are often drawn. Candidates must meet state ideological and professional criteria.

steps.title: Contractual Formalization
steps.description: The state agency signs the official employment contract with the worker. Simultaneously, the foreign company signs a 'Service Supply Contract' with the agency, specifying the roles, salaries (in hard currency), and management fees.

steps.title: Work Permit for Foreigners
steps.description: If hiring expatriates, you must obtain a 'Permiso de Trabajo' from the Ministry of Labor and Social Security (MTSS) and a specific business visa. This process can take 45-60 days.

steps.title: Orientation & Compliance Training
steps.description: Inducting the worker into the foreign company's operational standards while ensuring adherence to Cuba's Labor Code (Law 116), covering specific hours and required rest periods.

sections.title: Employment Cost Attribution (2025)
sections.subtitle: Estimating the Tripartite Financial Burden
sections.description: Costs in Cuba are complex due to the agency management fees and the discrepancy between the currency paid by the employer and the currency received by the employee.

sections.title: Strategic Employment Intelligence
sections.subtitle: Managing Risks in a Centrally Planned Economy
sections.description: Understanding the unique regulatory hurdles is vital for success in the Cuban market.

items.title: Dual Currency Risks
items.text: Foreign companies pay the agency in hard currency (MLC/USD), but the agency pays the workers in local CUP at official rates. This often leads to worker dissatisfaction and a need for 'incentive payments' which must be handled cautiously.

items.title: Law 118 Incentives
items.text: Foreign investment projects under Law 118 of 2014 enjoy specific labor tax exemptions during early-stage development, but only if they operate through a sanctioned Mixed Enterprise or IEAC.

items.title: Agency Selection
items.text: Choose your agency based on your sector. ACOREC is standard for general trade, while Palco is superior for high-profile events and diplomatic-adjacent business groups due to their logistical capabilities.

items.title: Permanent Establishment Risk
items.text: Using an EOR in Cuba does not shield you from Permanent Establishment (PE) risk if your employees are engaging in commercial contracts. You must ensure you have a 'Permiso de Establecimiento' from MINCEX.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.subtitle: Common Queries on Cuban EOR Solutions
sections.description: Addressing the most common concerns for foreign investors hiring in Cuba.

faqs.question: Can I pay my Cuban employees directly in USD?
faqs.answer: Legally, no. Official salaries must be paid through the employment agency. However, many foreign companies provide 'gratifications' or 'incentives' in kind or via separate accounts, which are complex and require local legal advice to structure compliantly.

faqs.question: What happens if I want to terminate an employee?
faqs.answer: The foreign company must request the 'discontinuance' of the service from the state agency. The agency handles the actual dismissal. Unless there is gross misconduct (as defined in Law 116), you may be liable for significant severance payments to the agency.

faqs.question: Are there private EORs in Cuba?
faqs.answer: There are no authorized private EORs for hiring Cuban nationals for foreign companies. You MUST use one of the government-mandated agencies. Beware of any service claiming otherwise.

faqs.question: How long is the probation period?
faqs.answer: Standard probation is 30 to 180 days, depending on the role's complexity, as specified in the agreement with the Cuban state agency.

sections.title: Cultural & Legal Nuances
sections.subtitle: Working Within the Cuban System
sections.description: Essential tips for managing a local workforce in Cuba.

items.title: The 13th Month
items.text: While not strictly mandatory in the same way as in some LatAm countries, it is customary for foreign companies to fund a year-end bonus through the agency.

items.title: Worker Councils
items.text: Trade unions ('Sindicatos') are centralized but very active. It is standard practice to consult with the local union representative on workplace conditions.

items.title: Political Sensitivities
items.text: Employment records in Cuba include evaluations of 'social behavior'. Ensure your HR practices respect local political sensitivities to maintain good relations with the state agency.

sections.title: Monthly Payroll Extraction & Disbursement
sections.subtitle: Standard Cycle for Foreign Entities
sections.description: Payroll in Cuba requires a high degree of coordination with the state employment agency and the Central Bank of Cuba (BCC).

steps.title: Gross Calculation
steps.description: Consolidate attendance data, overtime (25% surcharge for first 2 hours, 50% thereafter), and performance bonuses. Calculate the total in the currency defined in the Service Supply Contract (usually USD or EUR).

steps.title: Fund Transfer to Agency
steps.description: Transfer the total payroll amount plus agency management fees to the agency's account at the Banco Financiero Internacional (BFI). This must typically be done 5-7 days before month-end.

steps.title: Currency Conversion (Agency Side)
steps.description: The state agency converts the hard currency to Cuban Pesos (CUP) using the official exchange rate (currently 1 USD = 120 CUP, though variable) to prepare worker payments.

steps.title: Tax & Social Security Filing
steps.description: The agency executes the filing of Form 104 with ONAT. Social security contributions (14% employer) are deducted and sent to the national treasury.

steps.title: Disbursement & Pay Slip
steps.description: Workers receive their net pay in CUP into their local 'Tarjeta Magnética' (debit card). Digital pay slips must be issued in Spanish, detailing all deductions.

sections.title: Payroll Tax & Contribution Rates (2025)
sections.subtitle: Statutory Financial Obligations
sections.description: Summary of active rates under the Law of the Tax System (Law 113) and Law 118 for Foreign Investment.

sections.title: Payroll Compliance Insights
sections.subtitle: Avoiding Penalties in a Sensitive Market
sections.description: Critical alerts regarding Cuban payroll administration.

items.title: Reporting Deadlines
items.text: ONAT filings (Form 104) are strictly due by the 20th of each month. Late filings trigger immediate freezes on corporate bank accounts at the BFI.

items.title: Overtime Restrictions
items.text: Overtime is legally capped at 80 hours per year. Exceeding this requires specific justification to the Ministry of Labor (MTSS) or risk labor audits.

items.title: Annual Tax Recalculation
items.text: Every March, companies must perform an 'Ajuste de Impuestos' for the previous year. This often results in small credits or debits that must be settled via Form 105.

sections.title: Payroll FAQs
sections.subtitle: Common Hurdles and Solutions
sections.description: Clarifying currency and banking issues for foreign payroll in Cuba.

faqs.question: Which banks handle foreign payroll in Cuba?
faqs.answer: The primary banks are Banco Financiero Internacional (BFI) and Banco Internacional de Comercio S.A. (BICSA). Most foreign company operations must be domiciled here.

faqs.question: What is the 'Gratificación' system?
faqs.answer: Foreign entities often pay an extra amount to workers for performance. While technically part of the total cost, it is often managed via separate 'incentive cards' authorized for foreign workers, which have specific tax treatments.

faqs.question: How are sick days paid?
faqs.answer: The first 3 days are typically covered by the employer (through the agency); thereafter, the state social security system takes over at 60-90% of the base salary.

faqs.question: What is the currency of payment for social security?
faqs.answer: Social security (14%) is generally paid in the same currency as the service contract (USD/EUR) but converted at the official BCC rate for the agency's internal reporting.

faqs.question: Are year-end bonuses mandatory?
faqs.answer: The 'Aguinaldo' or 13th month is not strictly mandatory by the Labor Code but is a deeply rooted custom for foreign companies hiring through agencies.

sections.title: Payroll Reporting Essentials
sections.subtitle: Critical Documentation for ONAT
sections.description: Foreign entities must ensure their Cuban branch or the state agency maintains the following records for audit purposes.

items.title: Form 104 - Monthly Retentions
items.text: The primary monthly filing document where all employee personal income tax withholdings are declared.

items.title: Digital Signature (CIGES)
items.text: All payroll filings with the BFI and ONAT must be signed using the CIGES digital certificate issued by the Central Bank.

items.title: Overtime Approval Voucher
items.text: Any overtime paid must be backed by a 'Voucher de Autorización' signed by the local office manager to be deductible.

items.title: Variable Agency Fees
items.text: Agencies like ACOREC may reduce their 15% fee to 10% for large-scale infrastructure projects with 100+ employees.

items.title: Exchange Rate volatility
items.text: Calculations assume the official BCC rate. Be aware that the gap with the informal market price impacts your employees' actual purchasing power.

items.title: Annual Bonus Accrual
items.text: Add 8.33% to your monthly budget if you intend to pay a 13th-month bonus (Aguinaldo) at year-end.

steps.title: Determine Net Salary Target
steps.description: Research standard MLC rates for the role to ensure the worker is motivated despite the state currency conversion.

steps.title: Apply Agency Multiplier
steps.description: Contact ACOREC or Palco to confirm their current percentage fee for your specific sector (Trade vs. Tourism).

steps.title: Add Statutory On-Costs
steps.description: Calculate the 14% Social Security and 2% Special Contribution (if applicable) to reach the Total Cost of Employment (TCE).

faqs.question: Does the calculator include personal income tax (ISR)?
faqs.answer: Personal tax (approx 5%) is usually withheld from the worker's payout by the agency and is not an additional employer cost, but impacts net pay.

faqs.question: Are healthcare costs separate?
faqs.answer: No. Healthcare in Cuba is state-funded. The 14% social security contribution covers the employer's portion of worker welfare.

faqs.question: Is insurance included?
faqs.answer: Professional indemnity or specific workplace risk insurance is often managed by the state agency, but specialized riders may be needed for expats.

items.title: Hard Currency Liquidity
items.text: Ensure your Cuban bank account has sufficient MLC/USD liquidity 10 days before the pay date to avoid processing delays.

items.title: Minimum Wage Laws
items.text: The salary must meet or exceed the national minimum wage (currently 2,100 CUP) when converted at official rates.

items.title: Expense Reimbursement
items.text: Travel and subsistence expenses (Viáticos) are calculated separately and usually paid in CUP for local travel.

heroData.title: Entity Setup & Incorporation in Cuba
heroData.subtitle: Establish your legal presence under the Foreign Investment Law
heroData.description: Incorporation in Cuba is governed primarily by Law 118 (Foreign Investment Law). It is not a standardized 'walk-in' registry process; it requires high-level approval from the Council of Ministers or the Ministry of Foreign Trade and Investment (MINCEX). We guide you through the selection of the right modality and the complex licensing requirements.
heroData.bestFor: Strategic investors seeking long-term operations in Cuba

sections.title: Business Modalities in Cuba
sections.subtitle: Choosing the Right Legal Structure
sections.description: There are three primary ways foreign capital can enter the Cuban market under Law 118.

items.title: Mixed Enterprise (Empresa Mixta)
items.text: A joint venture between one or more foreign investors and one or more Cuban state-owned entities. It forms a new legal person (usually an S.A.) and is the most common form for large-scale projects.

items.title: IEAC (International Economic Association Contract)
items.text: A contractual partnership without the creation of a new legal entity. Used for hotel management, production management, and high-tech service sharing.

items.title: Totally Foreign Capital Entity (Empresa de Capital Totalmente Extranjero)
items.text: 100% foreign ownership. Can be established as a subsidiary of a foreign firm or a physical branch. This is the rarest form and usually reserved for technology or specific special zones like Mariel (ZEDM).

sections.title: The Incorporation Roadmap
sections.subtitle: Timeline: 4 - 8 Months
sections.description: The approval process involves multiple layers of the Cuban government.

steps.title: Negotiation & Intent
steps.description: Foreign investors must find a Cuban 'counterpart' (for JVs) and submit a 'Letter of Intent' to the relevant sector Ministry and MINCEX.

steps.title: Opportunity File Preparation
steps.description: Drafting the Feasibility Study, Market Analysis, and Technical Project. This must align with the 'Portfolio of Opportunities' published annually by MINCEX.

steps.title: Inter-Institutional Review
steps.description: The project is reviewed by a commission involving the Central Bank, Ministry of Economy, and Ministry of Labor to ensure it fits the 'Socialist Economic Plan'.

steps.title: Council of Ministers Approval
steps.description: Issuance of the 'Acuerdo del Consejo de Ministros' or the 'Resolución Ministerial', which serves as the final authorization to operate.

steps.title: Commercial Registry & NIF
steps.description: Registering the entity at the Registry Office of the Chamber of Commerce and obtaining the Tax ID (NIT) from ONAT.

sections.title: Estimated Incorporation Fees
sections.subtitle: Administrative and Legal Surcharges
sections.description: Fixed costs for registering a standard business presence in Cuba.

faqs.question: What is the minimum capital for a branch?
faqs.answer: There is no fixed minimum by law, but MINCEX usually expects a starting balance of at least $50,000 USD to prove solvency.

faqs.question: Can I own land in Cuba?
faqs.answer: Foreigners cannot own land outright. However, Law 118 allows for surface rights ('Derecho de Superficie') or usufruct for up to 50 years, renewable.

faqs.question: Is the Mariel Special Development Zone different?
faqs.answer: Yes. ZEDM (Mariel) has a 'One-Stop Shop' (Ventanilla Única) that drastically shortens incorporation time and offers significant tax holidays (0% income tax for 10 years).

faqs.question: How long does the incorporation process take?
faqs.answer: A standard process takes 4 to 8 months, but projects in the ZEDM can be approved in as little as 60 days.

faqs.question: Are multi-national subsidiaries permitted?
faqs.answer: Yes, but they must provide a full set of certified documents from their home country showing their financial history.

sections.title: Registration Requirements
sections.subtitle: Documentation Checklist
sections.description: The following documents must be legalized at the Cuban Consulate in your home country before submission.

items.title: Certificate of Good Standing
items.text: Issued by the parent company registry, not older than 6 months.

items.title: Bylaws (Estatutos)
items.text: A full certified copy of the company bylaws, translated into Spanish by an official translator.

items.title: Bank Reference Letter
items.text: A letter from a prime-rated bank confirming the solvency and account history of the foreign investor.

items.title: Power of Attorney (Mandato)
items.text: Specific power of attorney for the local representative to sign on behalf of the board.

heroData.title: Staffing and Talent Acquisition in Cuba
heroData.subtitle: Sourcing skilled professionals within a regulated environment
heroData.description: Accessing talent in Cuba requires a different approach than standard recruitment. We help foreign entities navigate the state agencies ('Canteras') to find specialized engineers, managers, and hospitality professionals. Our service focuses on candidate vetting, technical skills assessment, and liaison with the Cuban Ministry of Labor.
heroData.bestFor: Companies seeking high-skills technical or managerial talent

sections.title: Talent Sourcing Cycle
sections.subtitle: How to Find the Best Cuban Professionals

steps.title: Profile Submission
steps.description: The foreign entity submits a detailed Job Description to the state employment agency. The agency reviews it against their internal 'talent pool'.

steps.title: Pool Selection (Cantera)
steps.description: The agency provides a shortlist. You may also suggest names found through professional networks or LinkedIn (increasingly used by young Cuban professionals).

steps.title: Technical Interviews
steps.description: Conducting interviews (usually at the state agency premises or your authorized office). This is the time to assess soft skills and English/French proficiency.

steps.title: Security & Background Check
steps.description: The Cuban agency performs a 'Verificación Integral', checking criminal records and social standing. This is a mandatory state requirement.

items.title: LinkedIn in Cuba
items.text: Young tech talent in Havana is very active on LinkedIn. You can identify talent there first, then 'request' them through the state agency.

items.title: High Literacy Rate
items.text: Cuba has a nearly 100% literacy rate and produces thousands of high-quality engineers and doctors annually. Technical competence is generally very high.

items.title: Cadre Laws
items.text: Top management positions in major projects are often subject to 'Cadre Laws' (Ley de Cuadros), where the state has a more direct say in the appointment.

faqs.question: What are the most in-demand skills in Cuba?
faqs.answer: Currently, Renewable Energy technicians, Software Developers (Java/Python), and Bilingual Hospitality managers are in high demand.

faqs.question: Can I use external headhunters?
faqs.answer: You can use international headhunters to identify talent, but the final hiring must still go through the authorized Cuban employment agency.

faqs.question: Are background checks mandatory?
faqs.answer: Yes, every worker provided by a state agency undergoes a 'Verificación Integral' which includes criminal and social history.

faqs.question: Can I hire interns from Cuban universities?
faqs.answer: Direct internship contracts are difficult. Usually, internships are managed through an agreement between the foreign company and the specific university (e.g., UH or CUJAE).

sections.title: Recruitment & Placement Costs
sections.subtitle: Standard Agency Fees for Sourcing
sections.description: While agencies act as EOR, they also charge for the initial placement of specialized talent.

items.title: Worker File (Expediente)
items.text: Must include proof of educational credentials and the previous employer's evaluation.

items.title: Medical Clearance
items.text: All workers must have a current medical clearance (Chequeo Médico) from an authorized state clinic before starting.

items.title: Technical Skill Certification
items.text: For engineering roles, ensure the foreign company validates the degree with the Ministry of Higher Education (MES).

heroData.title: HRIS & Workforce Management in Cuba
heroData.subtitle: Bridging international HR standards with local state requirements
heroData.description: Managing human resources in Cuba requires tracking not just attendance and performance, but also the detailed records required by state employment agencies. Our HRIS solutions for Cuba are customized to handle dual-currency tracking, statutory reporting for ONAT, and interaction logs with agencies like ACOREC.
heroData.bestFor: International HR teams managing Cuban workforces

steps.title: Dual-Currency Mapping
steps.description: Configuring the system to record salaries in USD/EUR while generating pay slip previews in CUP according to the official BCC exchange rate.

steps.title: State Agency Reporting
steps.description: Automating the generation of monthly workforce movement reports required by agencies (ALTAS and BAJAS).

steps.title: Attendance & Leave Control
steps.description: Setting up thresholds for sick leave and unauthorized absences which must be reported to the state within 48 hours for disciplinary purposes.

items.title: Connectivity Issues
items.text: Cloud-based HRIS systems must have robust offline capabilities or local proxies due to intermittent internet connectivity in Cuba.

items.title: Data Privacy (Law 149)
items.text: Cuba's updated data privacy regulations require all personal information of Cuban employees to ideally be mirrored on servers within the country if possible, or heavily encrypted.

items.title: Role-Based Access Control
items.text: HRIS implementations must explicitly define access levels for state agency auditors, who may require limited view-only access to payroll logs during inspections.

faqs.question: Can I use Workday or SAP in Cuba?
faqs.answer: Yes, but they need custom local localization for the specific Tax and Labor laws of Cuba. Most 'out-of-the-box' Global HRIS do not support Cuba-specific payroll logic.

faqs.question: Is cloud hosting allowed for employee data?
faqs.answer: Yes, but data containing sensitive biographical information must be stored securely and meet the requirements of Law 149 (Protection of Personal Data).

faqs.question: Can the system generate the Form 104 automatically?
faqs.answer: Only if local Cubans modules are installed. Standard ERPs require a bridge software to format the XML for ONAT's portal.

sections.title: Implementation & License Costs
sections.subtitle: Budgeting for Digital HR in Cuba

items.title: Offline-First Design
items.text: Ensure your HRIS mobile app can cache attendance logs offline and sync once the worker is on a stable Nauta connection.

items.title: Bilingual Interface
items.text: While managers might use English, the self-service portal for Cuban staff MUST be in Spanish to comply with labor laws regarding accessibility.

items.title: Sanction-Neutral Hosting
items.text: Ensure your hosting provider (AWS, Azure) allows traffic from Cuban IP addresses, as some CDNs are blocked due to US sanctions.

heroData.title: Accounting Services in Cuba
heroData.subtitle: Financial compliance under Cuban Norms (NCIF)
heroData.description: Cuban accounting is governed by the Ministerio de Finanzas y Precios (MFP). All foreign entities must maintain books in Spanish and follow the Cuban Financial Reporting Standards (NCIF), which vary from IFRS in their treatment of currency unification, state assets, and fixed asset depreciation.

items.title: NCIF - The Local Standard
items.text: The Normas Cubanas de Información Financiera are mandatory. While they are moving toward harmonization with IFRS, specific 'resolutions' from the MFP take precedence.

items.title: Currency Unification
items.text: Accounting for assets purchased in CUC (now defunct) vs MLC vs CUP requires specialized historical revaluation entries sanctioned by the MFP.

items.title: Statutory Books
items.text: You must maintain physical or certified digital 'Libros Mayores' and 'Libros de Actas' in Spanish at the local office for sudden MFP audits.

sections.title: Monthly Closing Cycle
sections.subtitle: Timeline: First 10 days of the month

steps.title: Voucher Verification
steps.description: Ensuring all expenses are backed by official Cuban invoices (facturas) featuring the seller's NIT and stamp.

steps.title: Bank Reconciliation
steps.description: Reconciling BFI/BICSA accounts. Note that international wire transfers can have 'limbo' periods of 10-15 days due to intermediary bank blocks.

steps.title: ONAT Settlement
steps.description: Calculating Sales Tax (Impuesto sobre las Ventas) and withholding taxes for service providers.

faqs.question: Are digital signatures used for accounting?
faqs.answer: Yes, the Central Bank and ONAT use a specific digital signature certificate (CIGES) for official filings.

faqs.question: What is the penalty for late filings?
faqs.answer: Late filing of month-end balances can result in fines up to 5,000 CUP and the freezing of bank accounts until the filing is rectified.

faqs.question: Is consolidation with a foreign parent allowed?
faqs.answer: Yes, but you must maintain a separate Cuban set of books in CUP/MLC for local tax audits.

sections.title: Required Financial Statements
sections.subtitle: The 'Estados Financieros' Pack
sections.description: The Ministry of Finance and Prices (MFP) requires a standardized pack of four reports.

items.title: Estado de Situación
items.text: A standard Balance Sheet formatted according to the General Chart of Accounts of Cuba.

items.title: Estado de Rendimiento
items.text: Income statement highlighting the distinction between local and hard currency operations.

items.title: Asset Revaluation Entry
items.text: Specific entries required for any asset transferred from a Cuban state entity to a Mixed Enterprise.

steps.title: Chamber of Commerce Renewal
steps.description: Due every January. Requires submission of the previous year's financial summary and updated powers of attorney.

steps.title: MINCEX Operating Permit
steps.description: Must be renewed every 3 to 5 years depending on the modality. Requires an 'Action Plan' for the next period.

steps.title: Sanitary & Environmental Permits
steps.description: Required for any physical facility; regular inspections by CITMA (Environment Ministry) are standard.

items.title: Unauthorized Activities
items.text: The 'Objecto Social' is strictly enforced. If your license says 'Logistics' and you sell 'Software', you risk immediate license revocation.

items.title: New MSME Regulations
items.text: 2024 laws have tightened the relationship between foreign firms and private MSMEs. All contracts must be registered with the Ministry of Economy (MEP).

items.title: Anti-Money Laundering (AML)
items.text: Cuba's BICSA bank requires strict 'Know Your Customer' (KYC) documentation for all outbound MLC transfers to ensure compliance with GAFI (FATF) standards.

faqs.question: What happens if I miss a Chamber renewal?
faqs.answer: You may be temporarily removed from the Registry of Foreign Entities, meaning you cannot sign new commercial contracts until reinstated.

faqs.question: Are environmental impact studies required?
faqs.answer: Yes, for any project involving manufacturing or construction, a CITMA certificate is mandatory.

faqs.question: How often are tax audits conducted?
faqs.answer: Statutorily, every 2-3 years, but random 'fiscal controls' by ONAT can occur at any time.

items.title: Permiso de Establecimiento
items.text: The definitive document allowing a foreign company to keep a physical office in Cuba.

items.title: Libro de Actas
items.text: The corporate minute book must be bound and stamped by the Mercantile Registry (Registro Mercantil).

items.title: Legal Representative Permit
items.text: Ensure your designated representative has a valid work visa and a valid power of attorney recognized by the Cuban Consulate.

sections.title: Fiscal Strategy Insights
sections.subtitle: Navigating Cuba's Tax Incentives
sections.description: Understanding how to leverage Law 118 for tax optimization.

items.title: Dividend Tax Exemption
items.text: Under Law 118, foreign investors are 100% exempt from tax on dividends or profits reinvested in the country or repatriated.

items.title: Double Taxation
items.text: Cuba has a limited network of double tax treaties (approx. 10, including Spain, China, and Italy). Verify your home country status rigorously.

items.title: Special Regime for ZEDM
items.text: Companies in the Mariel Special Development Zone (ZEDM) enjoy a 0% tax rate on profits for the first 10 years of operation.

sections.title: Annual Tax Filing Process
sections.subtitle: Step-by-Step Submission to ONAT
sections.description: The cycle for corporate income tax (Impuesto sobre Utilidades) is strictly regulated.

steps.title: Fiscal Year Closure
steps.description: The fiscal year ends on December 31st. Accountants must reconcile all MLC and CUP accounts using the official year-end bank rates.

steps.title: Audit of Financial Statements
steps.description: Foreign entities must have their statements certified by a Cuban authorized audit firm (e.g., CANEC or Interaudit) before April 1st.

steps.title: DJ-02 Form Submission
steps.description: Submit the sworn declaration (Declaración Jurada) via the ONAT portal. Payment must be made within the 3 months following the close of the fiscal year.

faqs.question: What is the Social Security contribution rate?
faqs.answer: Employers pay 14% of the taxable salary base. This is paid monthly to ONAT.

faqs.question: Are there local city taxes?
faqs.answer: Yes, there is a 'Contribución Territorial para el Desarrollo Local' which is typically 1% of total income, though Law 118 investors may be exempt for initial years.

faqs.question: What currency is tax paid in?
faqs.answer: Taxes on income earned in MLC (hard currency) must be paid in MLC. Local operations in CUP pay in CUP.

items.title: NIT (Identificación Tributaria)
items.text: The Tax Identification Number is mandatory for all legal acts and bank account openings.

items.title: Vectores Fiscales
items.text: Every company receives a 'Vector Fiscal' which lists every specific tax they are obligated to pay and the monthly deadlines.

items.title: Electronic Payment Discount
items.text: Paying through the 'Transfermóvil' or 'Enzona' apps sometimes yields a 3% discount on personal tax obligations, though corporate use is still being refined.

heroData.title: MSA & Legal Frameworks in Cuba
heroData.subtitle: Contractual security in foreign investment
heroData.description: Master Service Agreements (MSAs) in Cuba must be elevated to a Public Deed (Escritura Pública) at the 'Consultoría Jurídica Internacional' (CJI) or another authorized state law firm. We handle the drafting and notarization of bilateral contracts, ensuring they are valid under both Cuban Law and agreed international arbitration (often Paris or Madrid).

items.title: Arbitration Clauses
items.text: Most complex contracts involve the Cuban Court of International Commercial Arbitration (CCACI) or specialized international bodies like the ICC in Paris.

items.title: Notarization Mandate
items.text: Any contract involving property or long-term investment MUST be signed before a Cuban Public Notary specializing in foreign investment matters.

items.title: Law Firm Selection
items.text: For intellectual property, specialized firms like LEX S.A. are often required to handle the OCPI (Patent Office) filings.

faqs.question: Are private law firms allowed?
faqs.answer: No. All legal services for foreign companies must be provided through state-authorized 'Consultorías Jurídicas' (e.g., BES, CJI, or Bufete Internacional).

faqs.question: How do I enforce a contract in Cuba?
faqs.answer: Enforcement is done through the Civil and Administrative chambers of the Provincial Courts or the Supreme Court (Tribunal Supremo Popular).

faqs.question: Can I use e-signatures for contracts?
faqs.answer: Cuban law recognizes digital signatures, but many state notaries still require physical wet-ink signatures for official deeds (Escrituras).

steps.title: Bilateral Negotiation
steps.description: Drafting the initial MOU or contract terms. Ensure the 'Cláusula de Resolución de Conflictos' (Conflict Resolution) is clearly defined.

steps.title: Consultoría Review
steps.description: Submit the draft to your authorized state law firm. They will ensure the contract does not violate 'Orden Público' (Public Order) or Law 118.

steps.title: Notarization (Escritura)
steps.description: Both parties appear before a Notary. The Notary verifies identity, authority (Powers), and reads the document aloud before signing.

items.title: Expropriation Insurance
items.text: Foreign investors can purchase insurance against political risk and expropriation, often backed by the Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA).

items.title: Helms-Burton Act
items.text: Be aware of Title III of the US Helms-Burton Act, which may affect companies operating on property confiscated during the 1959 revolution.

items.title: Intellectual Property
items.text: The OCPI (Cuban Office of Industrial Property) is efficient. Register your trademarks immediately upon entry to prevent 'trademark squatting'.

heroData.title: Software Solutions & IT Services in Cuba
heroData.subtitle: Leveraging Cuba's growing digital talent pool
heroData.description: Despite infrastructure challenges, Cuba has a thriving community of software developers. Since 2021, private Software MSMEs (MIPYMES) are authorized to export services and develop custom solutions for foreign entities. We bridge the gap, managing IT project compliance and export license requirements.
heroData.bestFor: Tech outsourcing and custom software development

items.title: High Tech MSMEs
items.text: Over 500 private companies now specialize in IT. They offer lower costs than regional neighbors but require specific 'Export Contracts' managed through state gateways like DESOFT or ETECSA.

items.title: Decree 370 & 371
items.text: Cybersecurity compliance is strict. All software developed for the Cuban market must pass a security certification by Segurmática to ensure data sovereignty.

items.title: University Partnerships
items.text: The UCI (University of Informatics Sciences) is the primary engine for talent. Collaborating with their 'Scientific-Technical Park' offers tax exemptions for R&D.

faqs.question: Can I hire a Cuban dev team directly?
faqs.answer: You can contract a private MSME, but payments must flow through the central banking system and technically involve an export intermediary if you are based outside Cuba.

faqs.question: Are cloud services available in Cuba?
faqs.answer: Local cloud hosting is provided by ETECSA (data centers in Havana). International cloud usage (AWS/Azure) is restricted by US sanctions/blocking.

faqs.question: What is the internet speed for dev work?
faqs.answer: Professional connections in Business Centers or shared offices (Coworkings) range from 20MB to 100MB, but residential connections remain slower.

steps.title: MSME Identification
steps.description: Select a private IT MSME registered with the Ministry of Economy. Verify their 'Sello de Empresa Digital' (Digital Company Seal).

steps.title: Intermediary Contract
steps.description: Engage an authorized state exporter (e.g., DESOFT or SOFTEL). They act as the financial bridge, taking a small commission (approx 2-5%) to handle the hard currency transfer.

steps.title: Milestone Validation
steps.description: Software delivery occurs via Git/Cloud. Once the client approves, the state exporter authorizes the release of funds to the MSME's MLC account.

items.title: Open Source Mandate
items.text: The Cuban government officially prioritizes Open Source (Linux, Python, Postgres) to avoid license dependency on sanction-sensitive firms.

items.title: VPN Requirements
items.text: Devs often require VPNs to access documentation or APIs (like Google Cloud Console) that are restricted due to US IP-blocking.

items.title: Offline Documentation
items.text: Encourage teams to maintain offline mirrors of standard libraries (e.g., MDN, Stack Overflow) to mitigate connectivity gaps.

heroData.title: Marketing & Branding in Cuba
heroData.subtitle: Navigating a non-commercial media landscape
heroData.description: Marketing in Cuba is unique. Traditional commercial TV ads are non-existent. Brand logic is driven by physical presence (BTL), state-owned radio, and the emerging 'Paquete Semanal' (offline digital distribution). We help brands find their voice in a market where 'socialist advertising' rules apply.
heroData.bestFor: Consumer brands entering the Cuban market

items.title: Offline Digital Ads
items.text: The 'Paquete Semanal' (Weekly Package) is a massive offline network for distributing media. Advertising here is incredibly effective for reaching the general public.

items.title: Advertising Law
items.text: Commercial advertising is strictly regulated. Highlighting 'luxurious' or 'exploitative' lifestyle is often rejected by state censors who prioritize 'socially useful' values.

items.title: Sponsorships
items.text: Sponsoring state-run cultural festivals (Jazz Plaza, Havana Film Festival) is the most prestigious way for a foreign brand to gain visibility.

steps.title: Creative Brief & Censorship Check
steps.description: Submit visual concepts to the ACC (Asociación Cubana de Comunicadores). They ensure symbols used (flags, figures) comply with the 'Ley de Símbolos Nacionales'.

steps.title: Channel Selection
steps.description: Choose between digital (MSME-led social media), BTL (Below The Line events at state hotels), or niche print (e.g., Opina or specialized trade mags).

steps.title: Media Placement Contract
steps.description: Sign a contract with state media entities like RTV Comercial for TV spots or ETECSA for SMS-marketing blasts to local mobile users.

faqs.question: Are there billboard ads in Cuba?
faqs.answer: Commercial billboards are rare. Most large-scale signage is reserved for political messaging or state-owned brands (e.g., Havana Club, Cubacel).

faqs.question: Is social media marketing effective?
faqs.answer: Yes, Instagram and Facebook are the dominant platforms for private businesses and brands. Audience engagement is very high compared to other markets.

faqs.question: Can I run Facebook Ads targeting Cuba?
faqs.answer: Meta restricts formal ad-buying targeting Cuban IPs due to US sanctions. Marketing is usually done organically or through local 'influencers' based on the island.

items.title: Nautical/Retro Aesthetics
items.text: Cuban consumers respond well to branding that mixes 1950s heritage with modern, clean digital designs.

items.title: Language Nuances
items.text: Use 'Español de Cuba'. Terms like 'Guagua' (Bus) or 'Asere' (Friend) should be used carefully depending on brand positioning.

items.title: QR Codes
items.text: QR codes are widely used in Havana restaurants and businesses to link to PDF menus or Telegram channels.
